data: Earth's only natural satellite and the only world other than Earth that humans have walked on. Its 1:1 tidal lock keeps the same hemisphere facing Earth at all times — the near side dominated by lava-flooded mare basins, the far side an ancient highland-cratered terrain crowned by the South Pole–Aitken basin, the largest impact structure in the solar system (~2,500 km wide, ~13 km deep). The Moon's slow recession from Earth (~3.8 cm/year) is gradually lengthening Earth's day; in the distant past it appeared nearly three times its current angular size in the sky.
Anorthosite highlands (calcium-aluminium silicates) + basaltic mare flooded by ancient lava; regolith depth 4–15 m; trace water ice in permanently-shadowed polar craters.
Luna 2 — USSR, 1959 (first artificial object on the Moon)
The Moon's orbit around Earth is the textbook two-body Keplerian system — every other moon-around-planet calculation generalises from here.
The Moon's 0.055 eccentricity is small but matters — at perigee the disc looks 12 % larger and brighter than at apogee ('supermoon').
Perigee (~363,000 km) and apogee (~405,000 km) drive the Moon's apparent size and the tidal-bulge phase that pulls the most water on Earth.
The Moon is unusually large relative to Earth — its diameter ratio (≈ 0.27) is the highest among the eight planets' moons.
An ellipse with the Sun at one focus — the simplest orbit a body can have around another.
How stretched the orbit is — zero is a perfect circle, one is a parabolic escape.
The two extreme points on every elliptical orbit: closest approach, and farthest.
Galileo's four-night observation in 1610 ended geocentrism. The system's moons are still ending old assumptions today.
